highlights.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
highlights.summary: OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world's most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.
body: CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

Much like Lanterns, Watchmen was met with mixed reception when it was first announced. Alan Moore's displeasure with adaptations of his work was well known at this point, and most fans asked why they should tune in when there was already a movie adaptation. highlights.summary: “3 Body Problem” and “Better Days” filmmaker Derek Tsang is attached to direct and executive produce “Group 41,” a true-crime drama series about the first Asian-American squad at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).
body: The project, from Jonah Greenberg ’s Salty Pictures, is at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

Over the next decade, the underfunded unit grows into an elite international task force. Its targets include Johnny Kon, a Hong Kong boss whose billion-dollar triad spans five continents; Johnny “Onionhead” Eng, a brutal Chinatown gangster; and Khun Sa, a warlord in the Golden Triangle with a 20,000-strong narco-army. The show explores immigration, prejudice and what the American Dream costs, with stories from both sides of the law.

Greenberg, a former managing director of CAA’s China office whose producing credits include Zhang Yimou’s “Shadow,” wrote the source book with Marc Iserlis and Aidan Swift, who are also producers and writers on the series. Greenberg says shows about present-day law enforcement can be great, but surveillance technology now gives cops the upper hand.
“Back in the 1980s when you went undercover, you went deep. And all the bad guys carry guns, and the danger to cops and informants is real,” Greenberg says.

highlights.title: Chris Packham: ‘When I was 14, I had a kestrel. I have never been happier or more in love since’
highlights.summary: The BBC presenter on listening to techno, wanting his ashes scattered with those of his dogs and shaving with his eyes shut. Born in Southampton, Chris Packham, 65, gained a zoology degree at the University of Southampton.
body: When were you happiest? When I was 14 years old I had a kestrel and I would get up before school to fly it. Nothing else happened that summer. My whole world revolved around that one bird and I have never been happier or more in love since.
What is the trait you most deplore in yourself? My mother used to call me the most tactless boy in the world. Don’t ask me what I think of your new haircut unless you really want the answer.
What is the trait you most deplore in others? Lack of honesty.
What would your superpower be? My mantra is: “Winning is not giving up.” If I’ve got to do something, it doesn’t matter what you throw at me, I won’t give up.

highlights.title: 38 Years Later, Calvin and Hobbes' Lost Character Remains Bill Watterson's Biggest Failure
highlights.summary: The author Lois McMaster Bujold has said that “the writer should always reserve the right to come up with a better idea.” That's a useful guideline for any reader to keep in mind.
body: Sometimes that decision is due to unexpected popularity, like how Opus and Bill the Cat quickly stole the spotlight in Bloom County. At other times, it might be due to shifting creative teams, real life concerns (i.e. Stephen King's near-death experience in 1999 became a major plot element of the last two books of his Dark Tower series), or that the author simply pivoted away from a plan that wasn't going to work out.

Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes has surprisingly few of those abandoned plot threads. It starts in close to the same place as it ends, as a joke-a-day strip with occasional deviations into high weirdness, art criticism, and accessible philosophy. There's a little more focus on Calvin's parents in the first couple of years of C&H and the art's a little looser, but the comic stays close to its original vision through its 10-year run.

The only real exception is in a two-week arc from 1988, where Calvin's uncle Max comes to visit his household. On a blind read through the comic, it's nothing that unusual, but the behind-the-scenes story of Uncle Max is a little more interesting.

highlights.title: Davika Hoorne Returning for ‘Inherit’ Sequel, Director Banjong Pisanthanakun Confirms (EXCLUSIVE)
highlights.summary: Banjong Pisanthanakun, the Thai director of horror hits “Shutter” and “Pee Mak,” tells Variety his new psychological horror film “Inherit” will get a sequel, with star Davika Hoorne set to return.
body: “Inherit,” a Centrepiece selection at the Toronto Film Festival, where it world premiered in September, is closing the Jakarta World Cinema festival.

Hoorne plays Woranart, a youthful-looking grandmother who moves in with her granddaughter’s wealthy family. The family soon discovers she harbors a centuries-old centipede spirit with sinister designs on the youngest in the household, Oui (Baipor Thitiya Jirapornsilp).

“The character has to be sexy, beautiful, and funny at the same time. I think of her as a fashion icon, too,” Pisanthanakun tells Variety. “The first image that I have was her wearing a bikini and sunbathing beside the pool, which is very modern. She talks like this [era’s] woman, talking to ChatGPT. She’s a very adaptable girl.”
On set, Pisanthanakun advised Hoorne to study Catherine Tramell, Sharon Stone’s character in “Basic Instinct,” and Anthony Hopkins’ Hannibal Lecter in “The Silence of the Lambs.”

highlights.title: ‘Minimal look, maximal politics’: why the black T-shirt signals modern power
highlights.summary: The look – worn by Abdul El-Sayed, Andy Burnham and Volodymyr Zelenskyy – radiates authority and no-nonsense masculinity, say fashion experts. For years the black T-shirt was consigned to the clothing category of plain basics. A hidden layer rather than the main event.
body: The progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who this week became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history, made a tight black T-shirt his signature look throughout his year-long campaign. Styling it with jeans and friendship bracelets made by his children, El-Sayed described his attire as “minimal look, maximal politics”.
In sharp contrast to the Maga aesthetic of boxy suits, El-Sayed’s T-shirt softens the lines between politics and the public. It’s anti-establishment without being alienating.
“Black radiates authority, seriousness, a certain no-nonsense masculinity,” says Johnny Davis, the luxury director of Esquire magazine.
A black T-shirt has also become a key part of Andy Burnham’s “man of the people” look – so much so that Kemi Badenoch once described the prime minister as a “pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt”.

highlights.title: How to predict the behavior of molecules from scant data
highlights.summary: A machine-learning approach called CheMeleon provides a practical way to develop new drugs or other molecules with much less detailed, expensive experimentation.
body: Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it’s pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs, or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it’s also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit.

Recent progress has been made on using artificial intelligence and machine learning to supplement or speed up laborious calculations based on physical principles that can at least provide some initial guidance on which compounds might be worth synthesizing and testing. Now, a new method developed at MIT shows that when there are few data on some technologically relevant property, such as ligand affinities for a recently discovered cellular target for a potential drug, this approach can outperform other existing methods for winnowing down the field of possible molecules that might be worth looking at.

highlights.title: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia
highlights.summary: Power and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago. In early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll.
body: As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process.

With the global rise of AI usage driving an increased demand for datacentres, south-east Asia has emerged as a surprise centre of growth in the Asia Pacific region. While China has the largest operational datacentre capacity in the region, a 2026 report by real estate firm Cushman and Wakefield shows that south-east Asia has the largest share of under-construction datacentre capacity in Asia Pacific, about 50% of the total. Malaysia and Thailand comprise a large portion of that capacity.

highlights.title: What we've been playing - "Sniffing out the warehouses on Prawn Island"
highlights.summary: Well, hello! I am once again wearing the Bertie hat in your usual host's absence, so joyous welcomes to our regular feature in which we talk about what we've been playing in recent times.
body: But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago. Bye!

Once again, I am finally playing a game from my backlog that I should've played years ago, and that's the delightful albeit dark card game Inscryption. There's so much more to this than you'd first expect, and I'm surprised the community has been able to keep the game's best bits under wraps for so long. Ultimately, nothing could've prepared me for Act 2, and my only real qualm with the whole experience is that I wish Act 2 had its own endless roguelike mode; you'd never be able to pull me away from it.

The game falters a little at the start of Act 3, I'll admit, and I've found myself very frustrated by what is an otherwise relatively easy time. This is down to me missing some rather useful earlier cards that I've since learnt would've made this final stretch much breezier, but oh well. I will still take down the Uberbots one way or another for the love of the game!

highlights.title: New Zealand reach Women’s Rugby League World Cup final as Waaka hat-trick sinks Samoa
highlights.summary: Kiwi Ferns defeat Fetu Samoa 32-0 in semi-final. Centre Waaka scores three of Kiwi Ferns’ seven tries. A Stacey Waaka hat-trick has helped secure New Zealand their place in the Women’s Rugby League World Cup final.
body: The Kiwi Ferns were rarely threatened in their 32-0 victory over an inexperienced Fetu Samoa in Newcastle, running away with it late with four tries in the final 12 minutes on Saturday afternoon. Dual international Waaka made the most of her opportunities, setting up New Zealand’s early first try, before securing three of her own. With her hat-trick, Waaka drew level with Australia winger Jaime Chapman atop the tournament’s tryscoring tally with nine.
New Zealand will now face the winner of Sunday afternoon’s semi-final between Australia and Fiji in Brisbane next weekend, as they look to avenge their 54-4 loss to the Jillaroos in the 2021 final.

The Kiwi Ferns drew first blood within two minutes, capitalising on a Samoan error to send winger Mackenze Wiki over out wide. In an otherwise error-marred first half, the Samoans had the better of the chances, but failed to register points in good territory.

highlights.title: Albania’s restored stone houses throw open the doors to visitors
highlights.summary: A project to convert the country’s traditional kulla houses into guesthouses offers a true flavour of ancient hospitality in a part of the country almost untouched by tourism. Sunlight pours through a tiny stone window, causing the wooden floorboards to creak as they warm up.
body: I’m staying in a kulla, one of the traditional stone tower houses that are found throughout northern Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia. They once protected families during times of conflict and sheltered weary travellers on trade routes, before mostly falling into disrepair in the 20th century. A new long-distance trail developed by the Albanian Agritourism Association aims to return some of them to their former glory and give visitors a chance to discover a part of Albania almost untouched by tourism.

The Tower Trail passes through some of the least visited areas of north-eastern Albania, with stops in the Mirdita, Mat, Bulqiza and Dibra regions. Designed to be walked with a guide over nine days, the journey spans more than 100 miles through traditional villages, high plains, forests and river valleys, with future plans for cycling and 4x4 routes. Some stages of the trail are long, and can easily be broken up into two days, or shortened with a car transfer. Opportunities to stay in guesthouses, farms and kullas help connect travellers with the cultural heritage of the region, in a way that is becoming increasingly difficult in more popular parts of the country.

They once protected families during times of conflict and sheltered weary travellers on trade routes, before mostly falling into disrepair in the 20th century.

highlights.title: The American Dream Wasn’t Built for Climate Change
highlights.summary: Owning a home is billed as a way to build wealth, but amid climate-related disasters, for many, it's beginning to feel like a trap.
body: This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

To Sierra Isley, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”

Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.
points: Owning a home is billed as a way to build wealth, but amid climate-related disasters, for many, it's beginning to feel like a trap.

highlights.title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
highlights.summary: An experiment in which AI models were asked to break into simulated networks showed the hacking skills of DeepSeek and GLM to be not far behind OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, which isn’t public.
body: Open-weight artificial intelligence models are now almost as capable of hacking into computer networks as the best closed ones, according to new research that heralds a much-anticipated turning point in the cybersecurity landscape.
Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.

“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.

The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.

body: The controversy flared because Dior positioned “Night in Color” as a celebration of traditional craftsmanship to launch its 2026 holiday season, drawing parallels between Chomet’s hand-drawn animation and the meticulous work of the house’s couture ateliers.

But Chomet and Soumache tell Variety that the film was created using traditional 2D animation techniques, with the characters, backgrounds and key poses drawn by artists. While they acknowledge using automated interpolation to generate some of the intermediate frames that make movement fluid, the pair insists that generative AI was never used to create the artwork.

“Some people are claiming Sylvain was contacted two weeks ago and that the entire film was made with generative AI, without a single drawing, but the reality is that this film took seven months to make and it was entirely drawn by artists,” says Soumache, adding that film employed roughly 20 people, including six animators, alongside storyboard artists, designers, background artists, compositors and editors.
“We used an automated interpolation system for a very small part of the process, but the film itself is traditional 2D animation,” says the French producer.

highlights.title: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls

TikTok is helping to promote and normalise the sex industry, allowing “sexfluencers” to post videos aimed at marketing pornographic content they have uploaded elsewhere on sites such as…
body: After studying non-explicit content posted on TikTok over the course of a year by some of OnlyFans’ most popular young female performers, researchers said the women buried coded references to pornography in “girly lifestyle content” that showed them shopping, playing with their pets, baking or offering skincare advice.

While mentioning OnlyFans or directly linking to OnlyFans from TikTok accounts is prohibited, euphemisms, emojis and crude gestures are used to indicate that performers’ adult content is available for sale on other platforms. TikTok prohibits sexual solicitation, including invitations to share explicit images, but the platform distributes so-called safe-for-work material produced by popular OnlyFans performers.

The report analyses how hints about adult content are hidden in widely shared TikToks that show OnlyFans stars filming their hair and makeup routine for “get ready with me” posts – known by the acronym GRWM. Performers may use the word “corn” instead of the word “porn”, or add the corn emoji next to a star emoji, to avoid the content being blocked.

highlights.title: Can AI really save you money on your heating bill? I spent two years testing to find out
highlights.summary: Samuel Gibbs doubted he could cut costs and still keep warm by putting tech in control. The results surprised him. Can smart thermostats and AI reduce your heating bills? Every manufacturer claims the answer is yes, quoting average savings in the 25%, or £180 a year range.
body: To find out if technology can really help, I spent the last two years comparing my miserly manual control and basic heating schedule to an AI-governed system. The results surprised me.
I used my 1930s solid-brick house with a recent, insulated loft conversion as the test bed.

In the winter of 2024 my heating system consisted of a 10-year-old Worcester Bosch combination gas boiler set to a medium heat, a Hive thermostat in a central hallway with its smart features disabled and 13 radiators equipped with standard thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs).

To maximise energy savings, I set a basic schedule to turn the heating on for a couple of hours in the morning and evening, turned off the TRVs in rooms we did not use and manually adjusted those in other rooms when we did not need them to be heated. I also manually turned the heating off when leaving the house.
points: Samuel Gibbs doubted he could cut costs and still keep warm by putting tech in control.

highlights.summary: On Tuesday, millions of American voters went to the polls and voted overwhelmingly for Democrats and against AI. The fight against Big Tech is about to come roaring back, and the fight over data centers is looking even harder for the folks trying to build them.
body: On The Vergecast: blue waves, the confusing business of AI search, and the many thoughts of RAM Altman.

On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David discuss what the 2026 midterms mean for the tech industry going forward. They dig into the self-quarantining echo chamber that is X, the congressional energy likely to be pointed at tech CEOs and AI regulation, and whether anything is actually likely to get done in the next two years.

After that, the hosts turn to AI. Specifically, whether anyone has figured out how to make money on AI. Specifically, whether OpenAI’s explosive growth in web search means much, when even Google can’t figure out how to make money on AI web search. Businesses are scaling back; agents don’t appear to be taking over. There’s a lot of money flowing around the AI world, but is there enough flowing into it to keep everything going? That’s the hard part.
Finally, it’s time for a somewhat abridged Brendan Carr Is a Dummy, the latest on SpaceX’s mobile ambitions, the touchscreen MacBook, RAM Altman, and much more.
